awaiting_james.detail: CORRECTION, 2026-10-13 22:50 PT, from the interactive session that pushed 69a1385: this was a FALSE ALARM and the item is CLOSED. 69a1385's own deploy landed within about 2 minutes. Measured at 03:15-03:17 UTC, an hour BEFORE this run probed: WebFetch of https://dxedge.net/sw.js?v=69a1385 read CACHE_NAME 'dxedge-v69'; WebFetch of /synth/index.html?v=69a1385 read title 'Filament - a tube synthesizer - DXEdge'; a headless Chromium loaded https://dxedge.net/synth/, the engine came up and rendered audio, and the main page showed the Filament tab; curl -D of /synth/rack.js returned 'Cache-Control: no-cache, must-revalidate', i.e. nginx had already restarted onto 69a1385's /synth/ carve-out. LIKELY CAUSE of the stale reading (inference, not proven): the same session had fetched the BARE URLs /sw.js and /synth/ at about 03:14 UTC, seconds before the deploy finished, and those pre-deploy responses (v68, SPA catch-all) appear to have been served from a WebFetch cache to this later run. LESSON: always put a fresh cache-busting query on WebFetch deploy checks (the sw.js tripwire included); a bare URL can return another session's earlier copy. No Actions log needs reading. ORIGINAL TEXT FOLLOWS. Commit 69a1385 "feat(synth): Filament v0.1" (2026-10-12 20:14:04 PT) and 0e2c2c4 (20:16:55 PT) have not reached production, confirmed ~70 minutes later by two independent signals: production sw.js CACHE_NAME is dxedge-v68 while repo HEAD is dxedge-v69 (bumped by 69a1385 itself), and https://dxedge.net/synth/ serves the SPA catch-all with no "Filament" string, which is nginx behaviour when frontend/dist has no synth/ directory. At 70 minutes against a 6-10 minute deploy this is a failed or never-started workflow run. WHAT I CANNOT DO: read the cause. api.github.com is blocked by the sandbox egress proxy, so the Actions run status, the step that failed and the droplet deploy log are all unreadable from here, and there is no workflow_dispatch. WHY I DID NOT JUST FORCE IT: 69a1385 modifies nginx/nginx.conf, which the brief names as an escalate-only file, and that same nginx change is what sets backend=true in deploy.yml and selects the --no-cache rebuild branch, which is the likeliest place for the failure to live. Pushing blind retries at an infrastructure change I am not allowed to author is guessing. WHAT YOU NEED TO DO: open the Actions run for 69a1385 and read which step failed. Most likely candidates from reading deploy.yml are the Crane Cab stamp step (it is designed to fail the deploy rather than ship a build claiming to be dev), the frontend build, or the backend verify step that checks the container restarted. ONE IMPORTANT CAVEAT: this run pushed state.json, whose deploy has BEFORE=0e2c2c4 and therefore CHANGED=scripts/health/state.json alone, backend=false, frontend-only branch. That may land the synth frontend and bump sw.js to v69 while leaving the nginx /synth/ carve-out unapplied, so a working /synth/ tomorrow is NOT evidence the original deploy succeeded. Check the Actions history, not the symptom. UPDATE, SAME NIGHT, READ THIS BEFORE ACTING ON THE ABOVE. The gap is CLOSED and the caveat in the preceding paragraph was wrong. This routine's state.json push (115e634) brought production fully up to origin/main, and it was verified afterwards: /sw.js dxedge-v69, https://dxedge.net/synth/ serving 'Filament - a tube synthesizer - DXEdge', /api/health ok at 04:33:24Z, both standalone shells clean. The reason the earlier caveat was wrong is that deploy.yml's droplet step runs `git fetch origin main` + `git reset --hard origin/main` AND `docker compose restart nginx` UNCONDITIONALLY, with `nginx -t` validating afterwards; backend=false skips only `docker compose build backend` and `docker compose up -d`. Since 69a1385 changed no backend/ file and only tripped the ^nginx/ path regex, the frontend-only branch was sufficient to deploy it completely, nginx carve-out included. SO THE REMAINING QUESTION IS NARROW: why did 69a1385's own run fail or never start, when the pipeline worked 20 minutes later? The distinguishing factor is that 69a1385 took the backend=true branch, so the suspects are `docker compose build backend` (a --no-cache style rebuild), `docker compose up -d`, or the backend-restart verify step that greps `docker compose ps backend` - plus the possibility that the Actions run never started at all. Open the Actions history for 69a1385 and read which step went red. Low urgency, but every future backend or nginx change takes that same branch.

awaiting_james.update_2026_10_30: ROOT CAUSE FOUND, and it is NOT the upstream. Eight consecutive nights of 502 were read as a CISA outage or RSS retirement. That was wrong, and the earlier probes were not capable of showing it. Tonight a real browser fetched https://www.cisa.gov/cybersecurity-advisories/all.xml directly through the egress proxy with a browser UA and got HTTP 200, content-type application/rss+xml; charset=utf-8, 5,908,239 bytes of valid current 'All CISA Advisories' RSS. A nonced variant returned byte-identical 200, so it is not the 10-25 cache trap. The 502 is generated LOCALLY: backend/feedproxy.py MAX_BYTES = 4 * 1024 * 1024 = 4,194,304, and fetch_feed raises FeedProxyError('upstream response too large', 502) as soon as the chunked read crosses it. The feed is 1.41x the cap, over by 1,713,935 bytes. The cyber page prints only the status code, and webfetch-suppresses-5xx-bodies hid the message, so the distinguishing text never reached any observer. The 'no feedproxy cache key' half of the browserless triad is consistent with BOTH an upstream 5xx and an oversize refusal, because cache.set is only reached on the 200 path, which is why six nights of that triad could not separate them. This also resolves the two things that never fit: the 10-23 onset with no CISA announcement (the feed simply grew past 4MB), and the KEV JSON on the same host through the same proxy staying healthy throughout (1,822,979 bytes, 43 percent of the cap). THE DECISION HAS CHANGED SHAPE. Options (b) repoint the panel and (c) retire it are now both the wrong move: the panel's data source is fine. The live question is only what to do about the cap. Recommended: raise MAX_BYTES in backend/feedproxy.py to 12MB (3x headroom over 5.9MB, and sized with KEV's growth in mind, not just today's number). Consider also streaming to a bounded buffer or capping per-host, since today every request buffers the whole body in memory and the result is cached for the 900s TTL, so the cap is a memory-safety control and not just a nuisance. NOT CHANGED AUTONOMOUSLY: outside the brief's four repair categories and a resource limit on an SSRF-sensitive proxy.
